# Designing the Future of Work — A Framework for Global Adoption

**Prepared for discussion by the Executive Committee, with People, Real Estate/Workplace, IT, Legal & Tax, and the regional Managing Directors in attendance.**

*Circulated for comment before any decision is sought. Figures marked "illustrative" are placeholders to be replaced once the discovery work in §12 reports. The principles, the allocation of discretion, and the decision requests in §14 are not placeholders — they are put forward for approval.*

---

## 0. Executive summary

**The situation, stated plainly.** We are being asked to settle a question that is usually framed as *"how many days in the office?"* — and that framing is, we would gently suggest, the reason so many companies have now announced three positions in four years. Attendance is an input. It is also the only input that is easy to count, which is why it tends to become the policy by default.

**The premise we would propose instead.** Location and schedule are not benefits to be granted or withdrawn. They are design variables in a production system, in exactly the way that layout, batch size and queue discipline are on a factory floor. The question is not *how much freedom can we tolerate*, but *what configuration of place, time and tooling gets the work done well, for whom, and at what cost to whom*.

**The organising idea, in one line:**

> **A thin global frame, a thick local fill — with the burden of justification resting on the restriction, and the burden of clarity resting on whoever holds the discretion.**

Very few things need to be true everywhere. A great deal needs to be decided close to the work. But — and this is the point most easily missed in a company headquartered in a low-context, individualist culture — **discretion that is merely permitted is not the same as discretion that is supplied.** In several of our largest markets, an employee will not act on a freedom that has not been visibly and specifically sanctioned by their manager. A framework that says only *"you decide"* will be read as generous in Amsterdam and as an abdication in Tokyo, Seoul, Mumbai and much of the Gulf.

**What we would ask colleagues to consider committing to:**

| | Commitment | Earned by | Target |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Stage 1** | Eight global invariants (§3) published, plus a mandatory **team charter** for every team of ≥4 | Discovery findings; regional legal review; works council consultation | Month 4 |
| **Stage 2** | Six contrasting pilot sites operating under the frame, with published results including the unflattering ones | Pilot instrumentation and honest reporting | Month 10 |
| **Stage 3** | Portfolio, tooling and reward decisions taken *on the evidence*, not ahead of it | Stage 2 evidence; lease expiry calendar | Month 12–24 |

**Illustrative investment ask (order of magnitude; to be firmed at Month 4):**

| Item | Year-1 cost | Note |
|---|---:|---|
| Discovery: instrumented listening in 12–15 countries, local-language facilitation, third-party interviewers | £0.6–0.9M | Non-negotiable prerequisite; see §12 |
| Common collaboration stack consolidation, decision-log and search layer | £1.5–3.0M | Consolidation should be broadly self-funding by Year 2 |
| Accessibility, bandwidth-floor and translation/transcription capability | £0.4–0.8M | The single highest-leverage equity spend, in our view |
| Workplace re-purposing (pilot sites only) | £2.0–4.0M | Deliberately *not* a portfolio-wide programme yet |
| Manager capability: outcome contracting, distributed team leadership | £1.0–1.8M | ~4,000 people managers, blended delivery |
| Home/remote work allowance harmonisation | Country-by-country | Legally mandated in several jurisdictions; not discretionary |
| Programme cell (5–6 people, deliberately small) | £0.9M/yr | See §11 on why small |
| **Total (Year 1, indicative)** | **£6.4–11.2M** | Against illustrative Year-2+ portfolio and attrition offsets of £15–30M/yr |

**Illustrative return.** On assumptions to be validated in discovery: portfolio efficiency of 20–35% of controllable occupancy cost as leases roll; a reduction in regretted attrition among high-performers of 2–4 points; access to talent markets currently closed to us; and a meeting-load reduction that is real money but that we would not attempt to monetise in front of this audience. *If discovery does not support the portfolio or retention figures, the correct recommendation is to adopt the near-zero-cost principles, decline the capital, and revisit in twelve months.*

**Decisions requested (also §14):** appoint a sponsor and a single accountable owner (Week 0); authorise discovery and works council consultation (Week 0); approve the eight invariants and the team charter mechanism (Month 4); approve pilot funding (Month 4); take portfolio and reward decisions only at Month 12+ (§10, §13).

---

## 1. How we would suggest this is taken forward

A framework of this kind does not succeed by being announced. Before anything is published company-wide, we would propose:

1. **Separate one-to-one conversations with each regional Managing Director**, in advance of any collective session, so each has the opportunity to shape the parts touching their markets before they are asked to endorse them in a room. Objections raised privately can be accommodated; objections raised publicly become positions.
2. **A short, sponsor-signed statement on the last two years** — that the reversals were failures of framing under uncertainty, not of anyone's judgement, and that **nobody's standing will be affected by having advocated a position that the evidence has since moved past.** This costs nothing and, in our view, is the precondition for candour rather than compliance.
3. **A published statement of what is *not* on the table**, settled in advance. Colleagues become markedly more inventive once they are confident the floor is solid:
   - safety, and physical presence where the work is physically bound;
   - regulatory, export-control and client-confidentiality obligations;
   - contractual customer commitments;
   - local employment law and collective agreements;
   - information security and data residency.
4. **Publication of every discovery finding**, including those unflattering to the sponsor, to the executive's own working preferences, and to headquarters. Particularly those.
5. **Deliberate design for indirect feedback.** In a good number of our markets, we will not be told what is wrong; we will be told that everything is fine, and then attrition will tell us later. Anonymous instrumentation, third-party interviewers, local-language facilitators and observed behaviour (§13) are not luxuries here — they are the only reliable channel.

The tone throughout should be that every regional practice we currently find odd is a rational response to conditions we have not yet troubled to understand. Those conditions are the thing to design around.

---

## 2. What we are actually deciding

It may help to separate four questions that are routinely collapsed into one, and to note that they belong to different owners and different timescales.

| Question | Really about | Decided by | Timescale |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Where** does work happen? | Place: home, office, third space, customer site, plant | Team charter, within the frame | Continuous |
| **When** does work happen? | Time: overlap, asynchrony, predictability | Team charter, within the frame | Continuous |
| **How** does work move? | Tooling, written record, decision rights | Global — genuinely | Months |
| **What is it worth?** | Pay, reward, career, status | Global policy, local law | 12–24 months |

Most of the corporate world's difficulty, we suspect, comes from answering the first question globally and the third question locally. We would propose the reverse.

---

## 3. The eight invariants — the thin global frame

These we would suggest apply everywhere, without local variation, and are the *only* things that do. Each carries an expiry date (§11).

**1. Design for the work, not for the room.**
Presence is required when the work requires it, and is otherwise a matter for the team. No global attendance quota. Quotas are a proxy for a diagnosis nobody has done.

**2. Distance is not the problem; asymmetry is.**
The failure mode of hybrid is not remoteness but a *two-tier meeting*: some in the room with the whiteboard and the corridor afterwards, some on a screen at the far end of the table. Therefore: for any gathering with at least one remote participant, **the meeting runs in the remote-inclusive format** — one person, one screen, one channel, or a properly equipped room with an accountable facilitator. This is a hard rule because it is the one everyone privately intends to break.

**3. Written by default; synchronous by exception, and earned.**
A global company that runs on meetings is a company that runs on whoever lives nearest headquarters. Decisions, rationale and dissent are recorded in a searchable place. A meeting is justified when the work is generative, relational, or contested — not when it is informational.

**4. A thin global frame, a thick local fill — subsidiarity as the default.**
Decisions sit at the lowest level that can see the whole of the work. **The burden of justification lies with the restriction, not with the freedom.** Anyone imposing a constraint above team level should be able to state, in writing, what breaks without it.

**5. Flexibility must be supplied, not merely permitted.**
Because permission is not culturally portable. Every manager states, explicitly and specifically, what their people may decide for themselves. "Use your judgement" is not a policy in most of the world; it is a test people are afraid to fail.

**6. Proximity must not pay.**
Promotion, pay progression, high-visibility assignment and access to sponsorship are monitored by working pattern and by location relative to leadership. Divergence is treated as a defect in the system, not a difference in the people. (§10)

**7. Nobody permanently absorbs the inconvenience of geography.**
Overlap windows are declared, recurring "awkward hour" meetings rotate across regions, and no region is structurally assigned the night shift for the convenience of another. Where rotation is impossible, the burden is explicitly compensated.

**8. Flexibility is redefined, not withdrawn, for location-bound work.**
Roughly [illustrative: 45–55%] of our people cannot choose where they work. For them, the currency is **time**: schedule predictability, shift-swap agency, advance rostering notice, and genuine choice within it. A framework that delivers freedom to knowledge workers and nothing to the plant, the lab, the field and the service centre would be worse than no framework at all — and would be read, correctly, as a statement about whose work we value.

---

## 4. Work archetypes — the analytical layer beneath the frame

Rather than classify *people* (by seniority, by role title, by "remote-eligible"), we would suggest classifying *work*. Most people do several of these in a week; the mix determines the pattern.

| Archetype | Characteristics | Place implication | Time implication |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Concentrated** | Individual, low interdependence, high cognitive load | Location-indifferent; home often superior | Fully asynchronous |
| **Coordinated production** | Interdependent, procedural, hand-off driven | Location-indifferent if instrumented | Async with a declared overlap window |
| **Generative** | Divergent, ambiguous, conflict-prone, trust-consuming | Periodic co-presence has genuine, measurable value | Intensive blocks, not weekly drip |
| **Relational** | Building trust with new colleagues, clients, partners | Co-presence, especially at the start of a relationship | Episodic, planned well ahead |
| **Apprenticeship** | Early-career, tacit-knowledge transfer, learning by overhearing | Proximity-dependent; the most under-priced item in every remote debate | Sustained, not episodic |
| **Response** | Incident, crisis, escalation | Location-indifferent; overlap-dependent | Follow-the-sun coverage |
| **Bound** | Plant, lab, hardware, clinical, retail, customer site | Fixed | Shift and roster design (Invariant 8) |

**The uncomfortable implication we would rather name early.** Concentrated and coordinated work argues for distribution. Apprenticeship and relational work argue for co-presence. Those two truths are both real, and they fall unevenly by age and tenure. A framework that optimises purely for the preferences of experienced staff will quietly disadvantage the people who have least voice in the consultation. We would suggest the early-career cohort is designed for *first*, deliberately, and that the design is a stated obligation of senior staff rather than a facility offered to juniors.

---

## 5. The local fill — how variation is handled without incoherence

Four layers, with explicit ownership. Anything not reserved to a higher layer belongs to the lower one.

| Layer | Owns | Constrained by |
|---|---|---|
| **Global** | The eight invariants; the common tool stack; pay architecture; the definitions used for measurement | Board |
| **Country / cluster** | Legal compliance, works council agreements, allowances, tax and PE guardrails, public-holiday and observance calendars, infrastructure floors | The invariants |
| **Team charter** | Anchor days, overlap window, response-time expectations, meeting norms, where and when co-presence is required, how decisions are recorded | The two layers above |
| **Individual** | Everything else, including how hours are arranged within the charter | The charter |

### 5.1 The team charter

We would propose this is the real instrument of the whole framework — one page, written by the team, signed by the manager, published where any colleague can read it, and reviewed twice a year. Seven questions:

1. What work do we do that genuinely benefits from being in the same room, and how often is that actually true?
2What is our declared overlap window, in every member's local time, and who absorbed the inconvenience of setting it?
3. What is our expected response time — and, more importantly, what is *not* expected? (When is nobody obliged to reply?)
4. Where do decisions get recorded, such that a colleague on the other side of the world can reconstruct the reasoning without asking anyone?
5.

# Lead Time Reduction Plan — Second Draft

**Prepared for review by the Managing Director and the three functional leaders (Production, Quality, Sales), with Engineering and Procurement in attendance.**
*Circulated for comment before any decision is sought. Numbers marked "illustrative" are placeholders to be replaced by the Week 6 business case; the governance, ownership and decision requests are not placeholders and are put forward for approval.*

---

## 0. Executive summary

**The situation, stated plainly but without attribution of fault.** We quote 14 weeks; our fastest competitor quotes 6; Sales reports losing roughly one deal in three on delivery. A previous attempt to compress the schedule produced a warranty spike that took two years to recover from. The three functions currently hold three different, internally coherent explanations of where the time goes. All three may well be partly right, which is precisely why no single function can resolve it.

**The central finding we expect the diagnostic to confirm.** In a build of this type, of a 14-week (≈70 working-day) quoted lead time, we estimate around **55 working days are waiting** — material queues, gate dwell, rework loops, administrative serialisation, and quote padding — and roughly **15 days are genuine value-adding work, of which the certified inspections themselves are about one day.** The prior compression episode, as best we can reconstruct it, compressed the 15 rather than the 55. That is the difference this plan turns on.

**The organising principle.** *Touch time is treated as sacred; queue time is fair game.* Every intervention must pass the test: *does this change what we inspect, or only when and how quickly the part reaches the inspector?* Where an intervention does change a control — and two of them do — it is presented openly as a **substitution of controls with equivalence evidence**, not as a free saving.

**The commitment we would ask colleagues to consider, in two deliberate stages:**

| | Quoted lead time (configure-to-order lane) | Earned by | Target date |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Stage 1** | **7 calendar weeks** (35 working days) | Flow, material, gate-dwell and rework improvements demonstrated in a pilot lane | Month 8 |
| **Stage 2** | **6 calendar weeks** (30 working days) | Demonstrated reduction in schedule variance permitting a smaller quote buffer | Month 14–16 |

Sales will understandably prefer to sell the endpoint immediately. It may be worth agreeing together that a **reliable 7 beats an optimistic 6**, and that the buffer is the last thing we spend, not the first.

**Illustrative investment ask (order of magnitude; to be firmed by Week 6):**

| Item | Year-1 cost | Working capital | Note |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Certified sub-assembly stock | — | £2.0–3.0M net | Gross £2.8–4.2M, reduced by aftermarket alignment (§10) |
| Inspection & metrology capacity (3 inspectors + 1 metrology technician) | £0.32M/yr | — | Recruitment lead time 3–6 months; interim third-party source inspection |
| Configurator (quote-to-BOM) | £0.25–0.45M | — | 6–9 months to live; **not** a quick win |
| eQMS / concurrent certification records | £0.30–0.60M | — | 9–12 months; registrar review required |
| In-process metrology, CMM programming, data capture | £0.40–0.70M | — | Phased by gate |
| MRP/ATP configuration | £0.12M | — | |
| Programme resource (lead + analyst) | £0.25M/yr | — | |
| **Total** | **£1.6–2.4M** | **£2.0–3.0M** | |

**Illustrative return.** On assumptions to be validated in Week 2 (200 qualified opportunities/yr, ~£180k average order value, ~37 losses/yr attributed to delivery, recovery of half of those falling in the fast lanes), incremental bookings of **£3.0–3.6M/yr** at ~30% contribution, plus **£0.4–0.7M/yr** of avoided rework, scrap and expedite cost, and a reduction in warranty exposure that we would not attempt to monetise in front of this audience. Indicative payback **20–26 months** including working capital. *If the Week 2 win/loss validation does not support the revenue figure, the correct recommendation is to fund only the near-zero-cost workstreams and stop.*

**Ownership — the change we believe matters most.** Today, end-to-end lead time is nobody's single measure, and each function is being asked to optimise something that makes it worse. We propose a named **Flow Owner** accountable for quoted lead time end-to-end, a weekly **Flow Council**, and a shared scorecard across all three leaders. Details in §2.

**Decisions requested (also listed in §14):** appoint sponsor and Flow Owner (Week 0); authorise the diagnostic and the certification enquiry (Week 0); approve the shared scorecard (Week 4); approve capital and working capital (Week 8, on the business case); approve Stage 1 quoting (Month 8, on pilot evidence).

---

## 1. How we would suggest this plan is taken forward

A plan of this kind will not succeed by being circulated and approved. Before the first Flow Council, we would propose:

1. **Separate one-to-one conversations** with the Production, Quality, Sales, Engineering and Procurement leaders, in seniority order, so that each has the opportunity to shape the parts touching their area *before* anything is presented collectively. Disagreements are far easier to accommodate at that stage than in a room.
2. **A short, sponsor-signed statement on the prior episode** — that it is now understood as a failure of system design under commercial pressure, not of individual judgement; and that **exercising quality stop authority will carry no career consequence, ever, and requires no escalation.** This costs nothing and, in our view, is the precondition for Quality's genuine (rather than formal) participation.
3. **A shared statement of what is not on the table**, agreed in advance: acceptance criteria, gate content, and stop authority. Once colleagues are confident these are secure, a great deal becomes discussable that is currently not.
4. **Publication of every diagnostic finding**, including those unflattering to whichever function commissioned the work, and including any that reflect on management scheduling practice.

The tone throughout should be that all three functions are currently doing what their measures ask of them. The measures are the problem we can change.

---

## 2. Governance, ownership and the alignment question

### 2.1 Structure

| Role | Holder (by position) | Accountability |
|---|---|---|
| **Executive sponsor** | Managing Director | Removes cross-functional deadlocks; signs the no-retribution statement; owns the funding case |
| **Flow Owner** (new, single point of accountability) | Director of Order Fulfilment (or equivalent senior appointment) | **Quoted and actual end-to-end lead time.** Convenes the Council; owns the plan; has release authority over the single sequence (§7D) |
| **Flow Council** | Flow Owner (chair), Production Manager, Quality Director, Sales Director, Engineering Manager, Procurement Manager | Weekly, 60 minutes, standing agenda: tripwire status, gate dwell, kit completeness, lane mix, escalations |
| **Escalation path** | Council → sponsor | Any item unresolved in Council is escalated with a written position from each function and **decided by the sponsor within 48 hours**. Silence is not consent; unresolved items do not simply age |
| **Quality Director** | — | Retains unconditional veto on anything touching gate content, sampling, or certification. This veto is not subject to Council majority |

Placing an explicit veto with Quality is deliberate. It is the mechanism by which speed becomes safe to pursue, and it should be stated in writing rather than assumed.

### 2.2 Shared scorecard — the substantive change

We would propose adding the following to **all three** functional leaders' scorecards, at equal weight, from the next review cycle:

| Measure | Definition |
|---|---|
| **OTIF against the *first* promised date** | Not the revised date. Re-promising is the mechanism by which delay currently becomes invisible |
| **Escape rate** | Defects found downstream of the gate that should have caught them |
| **Quoted-lead-time attainment** | Actual vs. quoted, by lane |

And, more delicately, we would suggest the sponsor consider retiring or neutralising three measures that are, we believe, generating the present friction rather than any individual doing so:

- **Production's utilisation / absorption target.** This measure rewards loading WIP onto the floor, and will quietly resist the WIP cap in §7D. It cannot survive alongside this plan. Suggested replacement: schedule adherence and throughput at the constraint.
- **Quality's inspections-completed throughput measure.** It discourages the very thing we need — inspectors idle at a gate, waiting, so that nothing else waits for them.
- **Sales' commission timing on booked orders regardless of deliverability.** Suggested adjustment: a portion of commission contingent on delivery to the first promised date, which aligns Sales with the lane discipline in §9.

We recognise these are compensation-adjacent matters requiring HR involvement and the sponsor's authority. We would not propose them lightly, but the arithmetic does not work without them.

---

## 3. Diagnostic: Weeks 0–4 (and what to do when the data does not exist)

### 3.1 Instruments

| Instrument | Method | Owner | Due |
|---|---|---|---|
| Order-level time ladder | Last 60–100 shipped orders: timestamp every state change from order receipt to ship | Programme analyst | Wk 3 |
| Touch-time vs. elapsed-time ratio | Standard hours ÷ elapsed working hours | Production Manager | Wk 3 |
| **Gate dwell decomposition** | Per gate: *waiting for inspector / inspection / waiting for sign-off / waiting for rework / re-inspection* | Quality Director | Wk 4 |
| Rework loop census | Every NCR: detected where, caused where, days lost, supplier or internal | Quality Director | Wk 4 |
| Material critical-path attribution | Which single line gated each kit? | Procurement Manager | Wk 3 |
| Quote-to-actual variance | By configuration family; exposes padding and whether padding is doing real work | Flow Owner | Wk 3 |
| Configuration Pareto | 24 months of orders clustered by option content | Engineering Manager | Wk 4 |

**Fallback, to be started in Week 0 in parallel rather than after disappointment:** if system timestamps prove absent or unreliable — which is common, and would be nobody's fault — we proceed with (a) manual traveller stamping on the next 20 orders released, (b) a full physical value-stream walk with the three functions present together, and (c) a two-day direct observation study at each certified gate. This yields sufficient resolution in four weeks and avoids eight weeks of data archaeology.

### 3.2 Two validations before any capital is committed

- **Win/loss validation (Owner: Sales Director, with an independent interviewer; due Week 2).** 15–20 structured interviews on lost deals. This is not scepticism toward Sales; lead time is simply the most available and least uncomfortable loss reason in any organisation, and if the true driver is price, reliability or specification, the capital in this plan is misdirected. Sales' credibility is *strengthened*, not exposed, by independent confirmation.
- **Competitor reliability benchmark (Owner: Sales Director; due Week 4).** Does the competitor actually *deliver* in 6 weeks, or quote it? If they routinely miss, then a guaranteed, penalty-backed 7 weeks may be a sharper weapon than an aspirational 6 — and considerably cheaper.

---

## 4. Where the 70 working days go

**Units, stated once and used throughout: all durations in this document are *working days* at 5 per week.** 14 weeks = 70 working days; the 6-week target = 30 working days. Calendar conversions are given in brackets where relevant.

Illustrative decomposition, to be replaced by the diagnostic:

| Segment | Working days | Of which value-adding |
|---|---:|---:|
| Order entry, configuration confirmation, engineering release, contract/credit admin | 7 | 1 |
| Purchasing cycle + longest-lead item wait to kit completion | 19 | 0 |
| Fabrication / machining queue and setup wait | 8 | 3 |
| Assembly | 7 | 5 |
| Certified gate dwell (4 gates) | 7 | 1 |
| Rework and re-inspection loops (probability-weighted) | 5 | 0 |
| Final test, burn-in, certification documentation pack | 6 | 4 |
| Preservation, crating, shipping preparation | 3 | 1 |
| Quote protection buffer | 8 | 0 |
| **Total** | **70 (14 weeks)** | **15** |

## 0. Executive summary

### 0.1 The situation, stated plainly

We are being asked to settle a question that is usually framed as *"how many days in the office?"* — and that framing is, we would gently suggest, the reason so many companies have now announced three positions in four years. Attendance is an input. It is also the only input that is easy to count, which is why it tends to become the policy by default.

### 0.2 Baseline — the facts the paper rests on

Colleagues rightly observed that the previous draft asked for money without ever stating the size of the thing being changed. Corrected:

| Baseline (FY-end; Finance, People and Real Estate systems) | Figure |
|---|---|
| Employees | **26,400** across **34 countries**, **118 sites**, 3.1M sq ft |
| Revenue | £4.8bn |
| Location-bound roles (plant, lab, field, service, retail, clinical) | **12,700 — 48%** |
| Non-bound roles (potentially pattern-flexible) | **13,700 — 52%** |
| People managers | **4,050** (of whom ~1,200 currently lead teams spanning ≥2 time zones) |
| Annual occupancy cost | **£96M**, of which **£74M** judged controllable within 5 years |
| Leases expiring | **22% by Month 24 · 38% by Month 36 · 61% by Month 60** |
| Regretted attrition, high-performer cohort | **11.4%** (three-year average 8.1%) |
| Works councils / collective agreements with co-determination on working time | **11 countries**, covering ~9,800 employees |

The lease expiry profile is the single most important number in the table. It means the portfolio question does not have to be answered this year — but 38% of it will be answered, by default, within three years whether we decide anything or not.

### 0.3 The premise we would propose instead

Location and schedule are not benefits to be granted or withdrawn. They are design variables in a production system, in exactly the way that layout, batch size and queue discipline are on a factory floor. The question is not *how much freedom can we tolerate*, but *what configuration of place, time and tooling gets the work done well, for whom, and at what cost to whom*.

### 0.4 The organising idea, in one line

> **A thin global frame, a thick local fill — with the burden of justification resting on the restriction, and the burden of clarity resting on whoever holds the discretion.**

Very few things need to be true everywhere. A great deal needs to be decided close to the work. But — and this is the point most easily missed in a company headquartered in a low-context, individualist culture — **discretion that is merely permitted is not the same as discretion that is supplied.** In several of our largest markets, an employee will not act on a freedom that has not been visibly and specifically sanctioned by their manager. A framework that says only *"you decide"* will be read as generous in Amsterdam and as an abdication in Tokyo, Seoul, Mumbai and much of the Gulf.

### 0.5 Staging — restructured

The previous draft proposed publishing globally at Month 4, "earned by" works council consultation. That sequence, as colleagues in People and Legal pointed out privately, would have been read in Germany, France, the Netherlands, Austria and the Nordics as a *fait accompli* presented for ratification — which is both legally exposed and, more damagingly, the fastest available way to lose the goodwill of the very bodies whose agreement we need. Revised:

| | Commitment | Earned by | Target |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Stage 0** | Nine invariants published as **stated management intent**, explicitly *not* as policy, with the sentence "local effective dates will be set jurisdiction by jurisdiction, following consultation" on the face of the document | ExCo approval; pre-notification to works council chairs *before* general publication | **Month 4** |
| **Stage 1** | Team charters live in jurisdictions where consultation is complete or not required (~15 countries, ~11,000 employees) | Local legal clearance; DPIA for §13 measurement | **Month 6–9** |
| **Stage 2** | Six contrasting pilot sites operating under the frame — **two of them bound-work sites** — with published results including the unflattering ones | Pilot instrumentation, honest reporting, matched-cohort design (§13.2) | **Month 12** |
| **Stage 3** | Co-determination jurisdictions live, on negotiated terms that may differ from the frame | Works council agreements (realistically **Month 12–24**, and not compressible by us) | **Month 12–24** |
| **Stage 4** | Portfolio, tooling and reward decisions taken *on the evidence*, aligned to lease expiry | Stage 2 evidence | **Month 15–36** |

Decoupling the announcement date from the local effective date costs us nothing and removes, we believe, the largest single execution risk in the plan.

The second draft's table under-stated the ask in three respects, all of which are corrected here: it omitted room technology despite making remote-inclusive meetings a hard rule; it under-scoped manager capability by a factor of roughly three; and it left the legally mandated home-working allowance outside the total. ### 0.7 The two lines that grew, and why we would rather say so now

**Room technology (line 4).** Invariant 2 makes remote-inclusive meeting format a hard rule. A hard rule that the estate cannot physically support is not a rule; it is an instruction to improvise. Our shared meeting-room count is approximately 640. Equipping the estate properly is therefore a **£11.5–22.4M commitment over four years**, of which we ask only the pilot tranche now. We would rather present that number to this room at the outset than discover it, one country at a time, when regional MDs are asked to fund it from their own budgets. Where rooms are not yet equipped, the exception ladder at §3, Invariant 2 applies — openly, not quietly.

**Allowance harmonisation (line 7).** Bounded: 13,700 non-bound employees, of whom an estimated 9,500–11,500 would qualify, at £30–65 per month depending on jurisdiction, gives a **steady-state recurring cost of £3.4–9.0M/yr**, with a part-year Year-1 effect of £2.4–4.5M. This is not an investment and should not be presented as one. It is a compliance cost that arises from hybrid working *already in place*, and it will arise whether or not this framework is approved. Our recommendation is that it be booked as a separate, non-discretionary compliance item so that it neither flatters nor distorts the business case — but that it be **visible in the same table**, because it is real money and colleagues in Finance will find it eventually.
